name: Habit
tagline: A quiet habit tracker using weekly targets and 8-week history instead of daily chains
summary: Habit is a single-person check-in log built with Next.js route handlers and Postgres (with PGlite for local dev). It uses weekly targets rather than daily streaks, archives habits instead of deleting them, and shows an 8-week history table. Auth is first-party with salted scrypt and opaque session t

built: Next.js route handlers for auth, data, and account deletion (src/app/api/*)
Weekly-target streak semantics and DST-immune Sunday–Saturday week arithmetic
Offline replay engine with queue supersession and five-retry drop policy (src/lib/sync.ts)
First-party auth: salted scrypt, opaque 32-byte session tokens, SHA-256 storage, per-IP rate limiting
PGlite in-process fallback for zero-config local development and test isolation
Opt-in Pulse mirror to localStorage with schemaVersion, placeholder-free rows, and timezone provenance

caseStudy.problem: Most habit apps optimize for initial engagement with daily chains that punish the first miss, causing abandonment. Users need a tracker that treats a missed day as information, not failure, and supports legitimate part-week habits.
caseStudy.approach: Weekly targets (e.g., 3×/week) with streaks counted in consecutive weeks met. The current week stays alive until it ends (Sunday–Saturday, DST-immune local calendar days). Habits archive with full history; deletion is explicit. Offline writes queue in IndexedDB, replay oldest-first, and supersede stale entries. First-party auth uses salted scrypt, httpOnly SameSite=Lax cookies storing only SHA-256 of tokens, with per-IP rate limiting. PGlite runs in-process when DATABASE_URL is absent, enabling zero-config local dev and tests. Schema changes are deliberate migrations (supabase/migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql). Pulse sharing is opt-in, mirroring to localStorage with schema versioning and deterministic ordering.

outcomes.statement: Weekly-target streak model keeps a habit's streak alive until the week ends, so a 3×/week habit can maintain a streak despite mid-week misses.
Zero-config local development and unit tests run against in-process PGlite with no external database service required.
First-party auth stores only SHA-256 of opaque session tokens, scopes every query by user id, and rate-limits credential endpoints.
Offline edits queue locally, replay oldest-first, supersede stale entries, and drop after five failures without blocking the queue.

tradeoffs.choice: PGlite fallback for local dev instead of a shared dev database
tradeoffs.gained: Zero-config onboarding; tests never reach a real database; CI needs no Postgres service
tradeoffs.gaveUp: Serverless deployments without DATABASE_URL lose all data between invocations because the WASM database lives on an ephemeral filesystem

tradeoffs.choice: Weekly targets (Sunday–Saturday) instead of rolling 7-day windows
tradeoffs.gained: Clear calendar alignment; streaks count whole weeks met; DST-immune local-day arithmetic
tradeoffs.gaveUp: Users who think in rolling windows must adapt to fixed calendar weeks

tradeoffs.choice: Opt-in Pulse mirror via localStorage rather than server-to-server sync
tradeoffs.gained: No shared database credentials; user controls sharing at the source; works offline
tradeoffs.gaveUp: Pulse only sees data from this browser/device; no cross-device sync of the mirror

lessons: In-process PGlite makes the test suite hermetic and fast, but the same fallback is dangerous in serverless if DATABASE_URL is missing — the README now warns explicitly.
Weekly targets with a live current week reduce the 'first miss' abandonment signal without gamification.
Storing only SHA-256 of session tokens limits blast radius of a database leak while keeping stateless cookie validation.
limitations: Single-user accounts only — no shared habits, families, or teams.
PGlite fallback is for development only; production requires a managed Postgres (e.g., Supabase pooler) and deliberate migrations.
Offline queue is per-browser; multi-device offline edits converge only when each device comes online.
Pulse mirror is localStorage-bound to one origin and one browser; clearing site data breaks the mirror until re-enabled.
